questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An aeroplane having a wing span of 30 m flies due north with the speed of 170 m/s. Magnetic field $B = 3.6 \times 10^{-5}$ T. The potential difference between the tips of the wings will be
questions.solution:
The potential difference induced between the tips of the wings is given by the formula for motional emf:

$E = B l v$

where $B$ is the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field, $l$ is the wing span, and $v$ is the speed of the aeroplane.

Substituting the given values:

$E = (3.6 \times 10^{-5}) \times 30 \times 170$

$E = 3.6 \times 10^{-5} \times 5100$

$E = 183.6 \times 10^{-3}$ V

$E = 183.6$ mV

Answer: $183.6$ mV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular disc of radius 20 cm is placed in uniform magnetic field of induction $\dfrac{7}{22}\ \text{Wb/m}^2$ in such a way that its axis makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with $\vec{B}$. The magnetic flux linked with the disc is $(\cos 60^\circ = 0.5)$
questions.solution:
Radius of the disc, $r = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$

Area of the disc, $A = \pi r^2 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times (0.2)^2 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.04 \text{ m}^2$

Magnetic field, $B = \dfrac{7}{22} \text{ Wb/m}^2$

Angle between the axis of the disc (area vector) and the magnetic field, $\theta = 60^\circ$

Magnetic flux linked with the disc is given by $\Phi = B A \cos \theta$

Substituting the values:

$\Phi = \dfrac{7}{22} \times \left( \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.04 \right) \times \cos 60^\circ$

$\Phi = 0.04 \times 0.5 = 0.02 \text{ Wb}$

Answer: $0.02$ Wb

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of effective area $3$ m$^2$ is placed at right angles to a magnetic field of induction $0.05$ Wb/m$^2$. If the field is decreased to $20\%$ of its original value in $10$ second, the e.m.f. induced in the coil will be
questions.solution:
Initial magnetic flux, $\Phi_1 = B_1 A = 0.05 \times 3 = 0.15$ Wb

Final magnetic field is $20\%$ of its original value, so $B_2 = 0.20 \times 0.05 = 0.01$ Wb/m$^2$

Final magnetic flux, $\Phi_2 = B_2 A = 0.01 \times 3 = 0.03$ Wb

Magnitude of induced e.m.f. is given by Faraday's law of induction:

$e = \left| -\dfrac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} \right| = \dfrac{\Phi_1 - \Phi_2}{\Delta t}$

Substituting the values:

$e = \dfrac{0.15 - 0.03}{10} = \dfrac{0.12}{10} = 0.012$ V

$e = 12$ mV

Answer: $12$ mV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The self inductance of an air-core inductor (solenoid) is $0.03$ mH. By introducing an iron core into inductor the self-inductance increases to $30$ mH. The relative permeability of the core used is
questions.solution:
The self-inductance of an air-core solenoid is given by $L_{0} = \mu_{0} n^{2} A l$.

When an iron core is introduced, the self-inductance becomes $L = \mu_{r} \mu_{0} n^{2} A l = \mu_{r} L_{0}$.

Given $L_{0} = 0.03 \text{ mH}$ and $L = 30 \text{ mH}$.

$\mu_{r} = \dfrac{L}{L_{0}} = \dfrac{30}{0.03} = 1000 = 10^{3}$.

Answer: $10^{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic energy stored in an inductor of inductance $4\,\text{H}$ carrying a current of $1.5$ A is
questions.solution:
The magnetic energy stored in an inductor is given by the formula:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2}LI^2$

Substituting the given values, $L = 4$ H and $I = 1.5$ A:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (1.5)^2$

$U = 2 \times 2.25$

$U = 4.5$ J

Converting to millijoules:

$U = 4.5 \times 1000$ mJ $= 4500$ mJ

Answer: $4500$ mJ

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solenoid is connected to a battery so that a steady current flows through it. If an iron core is inserted into the solenoid, then the current in the coil
options: may increase or decrease depending upon the direction of the current
questions.solution:
When an iron core is inserted into the solenoid, the magnetic permeability of the medium inside the solenoid increases.

This leads to an increase in the self-inductance $L$ of the solenoid, which in turn increases the magnetic flux linked with the coil.

According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction and Lenz's law, an induced emf is generated in the coil that opposes the increase in magnetic flux.

This induced emf acts in a direction opposite to the applied battery emf, thereby opposing the flow of the main current.

Therefore, the current in the coil will decrease while the iron core is being inserted.

Answer: will decrease

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils P and S have a mutual inductance of ($\pi$) mH. The secondary coil S has resistance $4\,\Omega$ and self inductance $(60/\pi)$ mH. If the current in the primary is $I_p = 12\sin(50\pi t)$, then the maximum value of the current induced in coil S is [Take $\pi^2 = 10$]
questions.solution:
The induced emf in the secondary coil is given by $e_s = -M \dfrac{dI_p}{dt}$.

Given $I_p = 12\sin(50\pi t)$, differentiating with respect to time gives $\dfrac{dI_p}{dt} = 600\pi \cos(50\pi t)$.

Substituting $M = \pi \times 10^{-3}$ H, we get:

$e_s = -(\pi \times 10^{-3}) \times 600\pi \cos(50\pi t) = -600\pi^2 \times 10^{-3} \cos(50\pi t)$

Using $\pi^2 = 10$, the maximum induced emf is $E_0 = 600 \times 10 \times 10^{-3} = 6$ V.

The angular frequency of the AC source is $\omega = 50\pi$ rad/s.

The inductive reactance of the secondary coil is $X_L = \omega L_s = 50\pi \times \dfrac{60}{\pi} \times 10^{-3} = 3\,\Omega$.

The impedance of the secondary coil is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\,\Omega$.

The maximum value of the induced current is $I_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{Z} = \dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2$ A.

Answer: $1.2$ A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Magnetic flux linked with the coil in weber is given by the equation $\Phi = 5t^2 + 6t + 11$. The e.m.f. induced in the coil in the $5^{\text{th}}$ second will be
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux is given by $\Phi = 5t^2 + 6t + 11$.

The e.m.f. induced in the $5^{\text{th}}$ second is the average e.m.f. from $t = 4$ s to $t = 5$ s.

The magnitude of the average induced e.m.f. is $e = \dfrac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Phi(5) - \Phi(4)}{5 - 4}$.

$\Phi(5) = 5(5)^2 + 6(5) + 11 = 125 + 30 + 11 = 166$ Wb

$\Phi(4) = 5(4)^2 + 6(4) + 11 = 80 + 24 + 11 = 115$ Wb

$e = \dfrac{166 - 115}{1} = 51$ V

Answer: $51$ V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider two coils in which a current in one coil carrying $6$ A causes the change in the flux in the second coil $12 \times 10^{-4}$ weber/turn. The second coil has $2000$ turns. The mutual inductance between the coils is
questions.solution:
The total flux linkage in the second coil is given by $\Phi_2 = N_2 \phi_2$.

Given $N_2 = 2000$ and $\phi_2 = 12 \times 10^{-4}$ Wb/turn.

$\Phi_2 = 2000 \times 12 \times 10^{-4} = 2.4$ Wb.

The mutual inductance $M$ is defined by the relation $\Phi_2 = M I_1$.

Given $I_1 = 6$ A.

$M = \dfrac{\Phi_2}{I_1} = \dfrac{2.4}{6} = 0.4$ H.

Answer: $0.4$ H

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two different coils have self-inductance $3L$ and $L$. The current in both the coils is increased at the same constant rate. At certain instant of time, the power given to the two coils is same. At that time there was current and voltage induced in the two coils. At the same instant, the ratio of energy stored in the first coil to that in the second coil is
questions.solution:
Let the self-inductances of the two coils be $L_1 = 3L$ and $L_2 = L$.

The rate of change of current is the same for both coils, so $\dfrac{di_1}{dt} = \dfrac{di_2}{dt}$.

The induced voltage in a coil is given by $V = L \dfrac{di}{dt}$.

For the two coils, the induced voltages are:
$V_1 = 3L \dfrac{di_1}{dt}$
$V_2 = L \dfrac{di_2}{dt}$

The power given to the coils is $P = Vi$. Since the power is the same at the given instant:
$P_1 = P_2$

$V_1 i_1 = V_2 i_2$

$3L \dfrac{di_1}{dt} i_1 = L \dfrac{di_2}{dt} i_2$

$3 i_1 = i_2$

The energy stored in an inductor is $U = \dfrac{1}{2} L i^2$.

The ratio of the energy stored in the first coil to that in the second coil is:
$\dfrac{U_1}{U_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} L_1 i_1^2}{\dfrac{1}{2} L_2 i_2^2}$

$\dfrac{U_1}{U_2} = \dfrac{3L}{L} \left( \dfrac{i_1}{i_2} \right)^2$

$\dfrac{U_1}{U_2} = 3 \left( \dfrac{1}{3} \right)^2 = \dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $1:3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The equivalent inductance between A and B is equal to
questions.solution:
Let the given terminals be Node A and Node B.

Let us trace the connections and identify the nodes in the circuit. We can label the junction between the $1\text{ H}$, $2\text{ H}$, and $3\text{ H}$ inductors as Node C, and the junction between the $3\text{ H}$ and $4\text{ H}$ inductors as Node D.

The top wire connects Node A to the top end of the $2\text{ H}$ inductor and to Node D. Therefore, Node A, the top end of the $2\text{ H}$ inductor, and Node D are all at the same electrical potential. We can consider them all as Node A.

The bottom wire connects Node C to Node B. Therefore, Node C and Node B are at the same electrical potential. We can consider Node C as Node B.

Now, let us analyze the connection of each inductor:
1. The $1\text{ H}$ inductor is connected between Node A and Node C (which is Node B).
2. The $2\text{ H}$ inductor is connected between the top wire (Node A) and Node C (Node B).
3. The $3\text{ H}$ inductor is connected between Node C (Node B) and Node D (Node A).
4. The $4\text{ H}$ inductor is connected between Node D (Node A) and Node B.

From this analysis, it is clear that all four inductors are connected in parallel across the terminals A and B.

The equivalent inductance $L_{eq}$ of inductors in parallel is given by:
$\dfrac{1}{L_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{L_1} + \dfrac{1}{L_2} + \dfrac{1}{L_3} + \dfrac{1}{L_4}$

Substituting the given values:
$\dfrac{1}{L_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{4}$

Taking the least common multiple of the denominators, which is $12$:
$\dfrac{1}{L_{eq}} = \dfrac{12 + 6 + 4 + 3}{12}$

$\dfrac{1}{L_{eq}} = \dfrac{25}{12}$

$L_{eq} = \dfrac{12}{25}\text{ H}$

Answer: $\dfrac{12}{25}$ H

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If current of 4 A produces magnetic flux of $3 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb through a coil of 400 turns, the energy stored in the coil will be
questions.solution:
Total magnetic flux linked with the coil is given by $\Phi = N \phi$

Substituting the given values:

$\Phi = 400 \times 3 \times 10^{-3} = 1.2$ Wb

The self-inductance of the coil is $L = \dfrac{\Phi}{I}$

$L = \dfrac{1.2}{4} = 0.3$ H

The energy stored in the coil is $U = \dfrac{1}{2} L I^2$

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.3 \times (4)^2 = 2.4$ J

Answer: $2.4$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils A and B have 180 and 360 turns respectively. The current of 1A flows through both the coils. Due to current of 1A in coil A, flux per turn of $0.8 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb is linked with coil A. Due to current of 1A in coil B, flux per turn of $1 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb is linked with coil B. The self inductance of coil A is $L_A$ and the self inductance of coil B is $L_B$. The ratio $L_A$ to $L_B$ is
questions.solution:
The self-inductance of a coil is given by $L = \dfrac{N \phi}{I}$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $\phi$ is the flux per turn, and $I$ is the current.

For coil A:
$L_A = \dfrac{N_A \phi_A}{I_A} = \dfrac{180 \times 0.8 \times 10^{-3}}{1} = 144 \times 10^{-3}$ H

For coil B:
$L_B = \dfrac{N_B \phi_B}{I_B} = \dfrac{360 \times 1 \times 10^{-3}}{1} = 360 \times 10^{-3}$ H

The ratio of their self-inductances is:
$\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = \dfrac{144 \times 10^{-3}}{360 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{144}{360} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic potential energy stored in a certain inductor is $49\ \text{mJ}$ when the current in the inductor is $70\ \text{mA}$. The inductance of the inductor is
questions.solution:
The magnetic potential energy stored in an inductor is given by:

$U = \dfrac{1}{2} L I^2$

Rearranging for inductance $L$:

$L = \dfrac{2U}{I^2}$

Substituting the given values $U = 49 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J}$ and $I = 70 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A}$:

$L = \dfrac{2 \times 49 \times 10^{-3}}{(70 \times 10^{-3})^2}$

$L = \dfrac{98 \times 10^{-3}}{4900 \times 10^{-6}}$

$L = \dfrac{98 \times 10^{-3}}{4.9 \times 10^{-3}}$

$L = 20\ \text{H}$

Answer: $20\ \text{H}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of $0.005\ \text{H}$. The current changes in the first coil according to equation $I = I_0\sin\omega t$, where $I_0 = 10\ \text{A}$ and $\omega = 60\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. The maximum values of e.m.f. in the second coil in volt will be
questions.solution:
The induced e.m.f. in the second coil is given by $e = -M \dfrac{dI}{dt}$.

Given $I = I_0\sin\omega t$, differentiating with respect to time gives $\dfrac{dI}{dt} = I_0\omega\cos\omega t$.

Thus, the induced e.m.f. is $e = -MI_0\omega\cos\omega t$.

The maximum value of e.m.f. is $e_{\text{max}} = MI_0\omega$.

Substituting the given values $M = 0.005\ \text{H}$, $I_0 = 10\ \text{A}$, and $\omega = 60\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$:

$e_{\text{max}} = 0.005 \times 10 \times 60\pi = 3\pi\ \text{V}$.

Answer: $3\pi$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the circuit shown, when the current '$i$' is $3\text{A}$ and increasing at the rate of $1\text{A/s}$ the measurement of the potential difference between A and B is $12\ \text{V}$. But when the same current $3\text{A}$ is decreasing at the rate of $1\text{A/s}$, the measured potential difference $V_{AB}$ between A and B is $6\text{V}$. The value of 'R' in the circuit is
questions.solution:
The potential difference between points A and B can be written using Kirchhoff's Voltage Law as:
$V_A - iR - L \dfrac{di}{dt} = V_B$
$\Rightarrow V_{AB} = V_A - V_B = iR + L \dfrac{di}{dt}$

Case 1: When the current is $3\text{ A}$ and increasing at $1\text{ A/s}$, we have $i = 3\text{ A}$ and $\dfrac{di}{dt} = 1\text{ A/s}$.
Given $V_{AB} = 12\text{ V}$, substituting the values:
$12 = 3R + L(1)$
$3R + L = 12$ ... (i)

Case 2: When the current is $3\text{ A}$ and decreasing at $1\text{ A/s}$, we have $i = 3\text{ A}$ and $\dfrac{di}{dt} = -1\text{ A/s}$.
Given $V_{AB} = 6\text{ V}$, substituting the values:
$6 = 3R + L(-1)$
$3R - L = 6$ ... (ii)

Adding equations (i) and (ii), we get:
$(3R + L) + (3R - L) = 12 + 6$
$6R = 18$
$R = 3\ \Omega$

Answer: $3\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight line conductor of length 0.4 m is moved with a speed of $7.0 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ perpendicular to magnetic field of intensity $0.8 \text{ Wb m}^{-2}$. The induced e.m.f. across the conductor is
questions.solution:
Given $l = 0.4 \text{ m}$, $v = 7.0 \text{ ms}^{-1}$, and $B = 0.8 \text{ Wb m}^{-2}$.

The induced e.m.f. across a straight conductor moving perpendicular to a magnetic field is given by $e = B l v$.

Substituting the given values:

$e = 0.8 \times 0.4 \times 7.0$

$e = 2.24 \text{ V}$

Answer: $2 \cdot 24$ V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils having self-inductance $L_1 = 75$ mH and $L_2 = 48$ mH are coupled with each other. If the mutual inductance of the coils is 37.2 mH, then coefficient of coupling will be
questions.solution:
The relation between mutual inductance $M$, self-inductances $L_1$ and $L_2$, and the coefficient of coupling $k$ is given by

$M = k \sqrt{L_1 L_2}$

Substituting the given values:

$37.2 = k \sqrt{75 \times 48}$

$37.2 = k \sqrt{3600}$

$37.2 = k \times 60$

$k = \dfrac{37.2}{60} = 0.62$

Answer: $0.62$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two planar concentric rings of metal wire having radii '$r_1$' and '$r_2$' (with $r_1 \gt  r_2$) are placed in air. The current 'I' is flowing through the coil of larger radius. The mutual inductance between the coils is given by ( $\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
Magnetic field at the center of the larger ring of radius $r_1$ carrying current $I$ is given by

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_1}$

Since $r_1 \gt r_2$, the magnetic field over the area of the smaller ring can be considered uniform and approximately equal to the field at the center.

Magnetic flux linked with the smaller ring of radius $r_2$ is

$\Phi = B \times A_2 = \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_1}\right) \times (\pi r_2^2)$

By definition of mutual inductance, $\Phi = M I$.

Equating the two expressions for flux, we get

$M I = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2 r_1} I$

$M = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2 r_1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0\pi\, r_2^2}{2\, r_1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils have self inductance $L_1$ and $L_2$. The current through them is increasing at constant rate. If the power dissipated in both the coils is same, then the ratio of energy stored in the coil having inductance $L_1$ to that in $L_2$ is
questions.solution:
Power supplied to an inductor is given by $P = |\varepsilon| i = L \dfrac{di}{dt} i$

Given that the current is increasing at a constant rate, $\dfrac{di_1}{dt} = \dfrac{di_2}{dt} = k$

Since the power dissipated in both coils is the same, $P_1 = P_2$

$L_1 k i_1 = L_2 k i_2 \Rightarrow L_1 i_1 = L_2 i_2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{i_1}{i_2} = \dfrac{L_2}{L_1}$

The energy stored in an inductor is $U = \dfrac{1}{2} L i^2$

The ratio of energy stored is $\dfrac{U_1}{U_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} L_1 i_1^2}{\dfrac{1}{2} L_2 i_2^2} = \dfrac{L_1}{L_2} \left( \dfrac{i_1}{i_2} \right)^2$

Substituting the ratio of currents, we get:

$\dfrac{U_1}{U_2} = \dfrac{L_1}{L_2} \left( \dfrac{L_2}{L_1} \right)^2 = \dfrac{L_2}{L_1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{L_2}{L_1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three coils of inductance, $L_1$ = 2 H, $L_2$ = 3 H and $L_3$ = 6 H are connected so that they are separated from each other. To obtain the effective inductance of $\dfrac{18}{11}$ H between points A and B, out of the following figures, the correct one is
questions.solution:
Given inductances are $L_1 = 2$ H, $L_2 = 3$ H, and $L_3 = 6$ H.

Let us calculate the equivalent inductance for each given circuit:

For circuit (P), the inductors are in series:
$L_{eq} = L_1 + L_2 + L_3 = 2 + 3 + 6 = 11$ H.

For circuit (Q), the inductors are in parallel:
$\dfrac{1}{L_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{L_1} + \dfrac{1}{L_2} + \dfrac{1}{L_3} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{3 + 2 + 1}{6} = 1$
$\Rightarrow L_{eq} = 1$ H.

For circuit (R), $L_1$ and $L_2$ are in series, and their combination is in parallel with $L_3$:
$L_{eq} = \dfrac{(L_1 + L_2)L_3}{(L_1 + L_2) + L_3} = \dfrac{(2 + 3) \times 6}{(2 + 3) + 6} = \dfrac{30}{11}$ H.

For circuit (S), $L_2$ and $L_3$ are in series, and their combination is in parallel with $L_1$:
$L_{eq} = \dfrac{L_1(L_2 + L_3)}{L_1 + (L_2 + L_3)} = \dfrac{2 \times (3 + 6)}{2 + (3 + 6)} = \dfrac{18}{11}$ H.

Thus, circuit (S) gives the required effective inductance of $\dfrac{18}{11}$ H.

Answer: $S$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the given circuit, if $dI/dt = -1\ \text{A/s}$ then the value of $V_{AB}$ at this instant will be
questions.solution:
Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) from point A to point B:

$V_A - IR - L \dfrac{dI}{dt} - V_{\text{battery}} = V_B$

Given:
$I = 2\ \text{A}$
$R = 6\ \Omega$
$L = 3\ \text{H}$
$\dfrac{dI}{dt} = -1\ \text{A/s}$
$V_{\text{battery}} = 6\ \text{V}$ (Moving from left to right along the bottom wire, the path goes from the positive to the negative terminal, so it is a potential drop)

Substituting the values into the KVL equation:

$V_A - (2)(6) - (3)(-1) - 6 = V_B$

$V_A - 12 + 3 - 6 = V_B$

$V_A - 15 = V_B$

$V_{AB} = V_A - V_B = 15\ \text{V}$

Answer: $15\text{V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A graph of magnetic flux ($\Phi$) versus current (I) is shown for four inductors A, B, C, D. The smallest value of self inductance is for inductor.
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux $\Phi$ linked with an inductor is related to the current $I$ by the equation:

$\Phi = LI$

where $L$ is the self-inductance.

From the equation, it is clear that the graph of $\Phi$ versus $I$ is a straight line passing through the origin, and its slope is equal to the self-inductance $L$.

$\text{Slope} = \dfrac{\Phi}{I} = L$

To find the inductor with the smallest self-inductance, we need to identify the line with the minimum slope.

From the given graph, the slopes of the lines are in the order:

$\text{Slope}_A \gt \text{Slope}_B \gt \text{Slope}_C \gt \text{Slope}_D$

Therefore, $L_A \gt L_B \gt L_C \gt L_D$.

Inductor D has the smallest slope and hence the smallest value of self-inductance.

Answer: D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular coil of radius 'r' is placed on another circular coil whose radius is 'R' and the current flowing through it is changing and their centers coincide. ($R \gg r$). If both the coils are coplanar, then the mutual inductance between them is proportional to
questions.solution:
Let the current in the larger coil of radius $R$ be $I$.

The magnetic field produced by the larger coil at its center is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.

Since $R \gg r$, the magnetic field can be considered uniform over the entire area of the smaller coil.

The magnetic flux linked with the smaller coil of radius $r$ is $\Phi = B A = \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}\right) (\pi r^2)$.

The mutual inductance $M$ is given by $M = \dfrac{\Phi}{I} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{2R}$.

Therefore, $M \propto \dfrac{r^2}{R}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{r^2}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal rod of length 'L' completes the circuit as shown. The area of the circuit is perpendicular to magnetic field 'B'. Total resistance of the circuit is 'R'. The force needed to move the rod in the direction as shown with constant speed 'V' is
questions.solution:
When the metal rod of length $L$ moves with a velocity $V$ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$, a motional emf is induced across its ends.

The induced emf is given by:
$E = BVL$

This emf drives an induced current $I$ through the circuit with total resistance $R$:
$I = \dfrac{E}{R} = \dfrac{BVL}{R}$

The current-carrying rod experiences a magnetic force $F_m$ opposing its motion (due to Lenz's Law), which is given by:
$F_m = ILB$

Substituting the value of $I$ into the force equation:
$F_m = \left(\dfrac{BVL}{R}\right)LB = \dfrac{B^2L^2V}{R}$

To move the rod with a constant speed $V$, the net force must be zero. Therefore, the external force $F$ needed must be equal in magnitude to the magnetic force:
$F = F_m = \dfrac{B^2L^2V}{R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\text{B}^2\text{L}^2\text{V}}{\text{R}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two solenoids A and B of equal number of turns have their lengths and radii in the same ratio $1 : 3$. The ratio of the self-inductance of solenoid A to that of B will be
questions.solution:
The self-inductance of a solenoid is given by the formula $L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 \pi r^2}{l}$

Given that the number of turns are equal, $N_A = N_B$.

The ratio of their lengths is $\dfrac{l_A}{l_B} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

The ratio of their radii is $\dfrac{r_A}{r_B} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Taking the ratio of their self-inductances:

$\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = \left(\dfrac{r_A}{r_B}\right)^2 \times \dfrac{l_B}{l_A}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{1}\right)$

$\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = \dfrac{1}{9} \times 3 = \dfrac{1}{3}$

The ratio of the self-inductance of solenoid A to that of B is $1 : 3$.

Answer: $1 : 3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two concentric circular coils having radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ ($r_2 \lt \lt  r_1$) are placed co-axially with centres coinciding. The mutual inductance of the arrangement is (Both coils have single turn, $\mu_0$ = permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
Let a current $I$ flow through the outer coil of radius $r_1$.

The magnetic field at the centre of the outer coil is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r_1}$.

Since $r_2 \lt \lt r_1$, this magnetic field can be considered uniform over the entire area of the inner coil.

The magnetic flux linked with the inner coil of radius $r_2$ is $\Phi = B \times A = \left(\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r_1}\right) \times (\pi r_2^2)$.

The mutual inductance $M$ of the arrangement is defined as $M = \dfrac{\Phi}{I}$.

Substituting the value of $\Phi$, we get $M = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2r_1}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\mu_0 r_2^2 \pi}{2r_1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bar magnet falls from a height 'h' through a metal pipe, its acceleration after coming out of pipe is
questions.solution:
When the bar magnet falls through the metal pipe, the changing magnetic flux induces eddy currents in the pipe.

According to Lenz's law, these eddy currents oppose the motion of the magnet, making its acceleration less than $g$ ($9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$) while inside the pipe.

Once the magnet comes out of the pipe, there is no induced current to oppose its motion.

The only force acting on the magnet is gravity.

Therefore, its acceleration after coming out of the pipe is equal to the acceleration due to gravity, which is $9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The coefficient of mutual induction is $3$H and induced e.m.f. across secondary is $4$ kV. Current in primary is reduced from $7$A to $2$A. The time required for the change of current is
questions.solution:
The magnitude of induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil is given by

$|e| = M \left| \dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \right|$

Substituting the given values:

$4000 = 3 \times \left| \dfrac{2 - 7}{\Delta t} \right|$

$4000 = \dfrac{15}{\Delta t}$

$\Delta t = \dfrac{15}{4000} = 3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ s

Answer: $3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of 'n' turns and resistance $R\,\Omega$ is connected in series with a resistance $R/4$. The combination is moved for time 't' second through flux $\Phi_1$ to $\Phi_2$. The induced current in the circuit is
questions.solution:
The total resistance of the circuit is given by the sum of the coil's resistance and the series resistance:

$R_{eq} = R + \dfrac{R}{4} = \dfrac{5R}{4}$

According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the average induced emf in a coil of $n$ turns is:

$E = -n \dfrac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = -n \dfrac{\Phi_2 - \Phi_1}{t} = \dfrac{n(\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{t}$

The induced current in the circuit is the ratio of the induced emf to the total resistance:

$I = \dfrac{E}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{n(\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{t}}{\dfrac{5R}{4}} = \dfrac{4n(\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{5Rt}$

Using $T$ for time as given in the options, the induced current is $\dfrac{4n(\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{5RT}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A conducting loop of radius $10/[\pi]^{1/2}$ cm is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $0.5$ T. The magnetic field is decreased to zero in $0.5$ s at a steady rate. The induced emf in the circular loop at $0.25$ s is
questions.solution:
Given radius of the loop, $r = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{\pi}}\text{ cm} = \dfrac{0.1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\text{ m}$

Area of the loop, $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \left(\dfrac{0.1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^2 = 0.01\text{ m}^2$

Initial magnetic field, $B_i = 0.5\text{ T}$

Final magnetic field, $B_f = 0\text{ T}$

Time interval, $\Delta t = 0.5\text{ s}$

Since the magnetic field decreases at a steady rate, the rate of change of magnetic field is constant.

$\dfrac{dB}{dt} = \dfrac{B_f - B_i}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0 - 0.5}{0.5} = -1\text{ T/s}$

According to Faraday's law of induction, the induced emf is given by:

$e = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = -A \dfrac{dB}{dt}$

$e = -0.01 \times (-1) = 0.01\text{ V} = 10\text{ mV}$

Since the rate of change of magnetic field is constant, the induced emf is constant at all times during the interval. Thus, the induced emf at $t = 0.25\text{ s}$ is $10\text{ mV}$.

Answer: $10\text{ mV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils P and Q have mutual inductance 'M' H. If the current in the coil P is $I = I_0 \sin \omega t$, then the maximum value of e.m.f. induced in coil Q is
questions.solution:
The induced e.m.f. in coil Q due to the current in coil P is given by

$e = -M \dfrac{dI}{dt}$

Given $I = I_0 \sin \omega t$, differentiating with respect to time $t$ gives

$\dfrac{dI}{dt} = I_0 \omega \cos \omega t$

Substituting this into the expression for induced e.m.f.,

$e = -M I_0 \omega \cos \omega t$

The maximum value of the induced e.m.f. corresponds to the maximum magnitude of $\cos \omega t$, which is $1$.

$e_{\text{max}} = M \omega I_0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The current flowing through the inductor of self inductance 'L' is continuously increasing at constant rate. The variation of induced e.m.f. (e) versus $\dfrac{dI}{dt}$ is shown graphically by figure
questions.solution:
The induced electromotive force (e.m.f.) in an inductor is given by Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, which incorporates Lenz's law:

$e = -L \dfrac{dI}{dt}$

Here, $e$ is the induced e.m.f., $L$ is the self-inductance of the coil, and $\dfrac{dI}{dt}$ is the rate of change of current.

Comparing this equation with the standard equation of a straight line passing through the origin, $y = mx$:
We have $y = e$ and $x = \dfrac{dI}{dt}$.
The slope of the line is $m = -L$.

Since the self-inductance $L$ is a positive constant, the slope $m$ is negative. Therefore, the graph of $e$ versus $\dfrac{dI}{dt}$ will be a straight line passing through the origin with a negative slope. As $\dfrac{dI}{dt}$ is positive (current is increasing), $e$ will be negative.

This linear relationship with a negative slope is correctly represented by the graph in figure C.

Answer: C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil having 'n' turns and resistance 'R' is connected with a galvanometer of resistance '2R'. This combination is moved in time 't' from flux $\phi_1$ to $\phi_2$ Wb. The induced current in the circuit is
questions.solution:
The total resistance of the circuit is the sum of the resistance of the coil and the galvanometer.

$R_{eq} = R + 2R = 3R$

According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the magnitude of the average induced emf is given by the rate of change of total magnetic flux:

$|E| = n \dfrac{|\Delta \phi|}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{n(\phi_2 - \phi_1)}{t}$

The induced current in the circuit is the ratio of the induced emf to the total resistance:

$I = \dfrac{|E|}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{n(\phi_2 - \phi_1)}{3Rt}$

Answer: $\dfrac{n(\phi_2 - \phi_1)}{3Rt}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The following figure represents two bulbs $B_1$ and $B_2$, resistor R and an inductor L. When the switch S is turned off, which of the following statement is true?
options: $B_1$ becomes off promptly but $B_2$ with some delay
$B_2$ becomes off promptly but $B_1$ with some delay
Both $B_1$ and $B_2$ becomes off with same delay
questions.solution:
When the switch S is turned off, the main voltage source is disconnected from the circuit.

The inductor L has stored energy in its magnetic field. According to Faraday's and Lenz's laws, it opposes the sudden drop in current and acts as a source of emf.

A closed loop is formed containing the inductor L, bulb $B_2$, bulb $B_1$, and resistor R in series.

The induced current from the inductor flows through this series loop, meaning the same decaying current passes through both bulbs $B_1$ and $B_2$.

Since the current through both bulbs is identical at any instant after the switch is opened, both $B_1$ and $B_2$ become off with the same delay.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long rectangular conducting loop of width '$l$' mass '$m$' and resistance '$R$' is placed partly in a perpendicular magnetic field '$B$'. With what velocity should it be pushed downwards so that it may continue to fall without any acceleration? ($g$ = acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
When the loop falls with a velocity $v$, the motional emf induced in the top horizontal segment of the loop is given by:

$\varepsilon = Bvl$

The induced current in the loop is:

$I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} = \dfrac{Bvl}{R}$

This current experiences an upward magnetic force due to the magnetic field $B$. The magnitude of this force is:

$F_m = IlB = \left(\dfrac{Bvl}{R}\right)lB = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$

For the loop to fall without any acceleration, the net force on it must be zero. Therefore, the upward magnetic force must balance the downward gravitational force:

$F_m = mg$

$\dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R} = mg$

Solving for $v$, we get:

$v = \dfrac{mgR}{B^2l^2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{mgR}{B^2 l^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square loop of area $25 \text{ cm}^2$ has a resistance of $10\Omega$. The loop is placed in uniform magnetic field of magnitude $40$ T. The plane of the loop is perpendicular to the magnetic field. The work done in pulling the loop out of the magnetic field slowly and uniformly in one second will be
questions.solution:
Given:
Area of the loop, $A = 25 \text{ cm}^2 = 25 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$
Resistance, $R = 10 \ \Omega$
Magnetic field, $B = 40 \text{ T}$
Time taken, $\Delta t = 1 \text{ s}$

The total change in magnetic flux as the loop is pulled out of the magnetic field is:
$\Delta \Phi = B A = 40 \times 25 \times 10^{-4} = 0.1 \text{ Wb}$

Since the loop is pulled out uniformly, the rate of change of flux is constant. The induced emf $E$ is:
$E = \dfrac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0.1}{1} = 0.1 \text{ V}$

The electrical power dissipated as heat in the loop due to its resistance is:
$P = \dfrac{E^2}{R} = \dfrac{(0.1)^2}{10} = \dfrac{0.01}{10} = 10^{-3} \text{ W}$

The work done by the external agent in pulling the loop out slowly and uniformly is equal to the total heat energy dissipated:
$W = P \Delta t = 10^{-3} \times 1 = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J}$

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two inductors of 80 mH each are joined in parallel. The current passing through the combination is 2.1 A . The energy stored in this combination of inductors is
questions.solution:
Energy stored in parallel inductor combination

For two identical inductors $L_1 = L_2 = L = 80 \times 10^{-3}$ H connected in parallel, the equivalent inductance is $L_{eq} = \frac{L}{2} = 40 \times 10^{-3}$ H.

The energy stored in an inductor carrying current $I = 2.1$ A is given by $U = \frac{1}{2} L_{eq} I^2$. Substituting values:

$U = \frac{1}{2} (40 \times 10^{-3}) (2.1)^2 = \frac{1}{2} (40 \times 10^{-3}) (4.41) = 88.2 \times 10^{-3} = 8.82 \times 10^{-2}$ J

This matches option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of effective area $3 \mathrm{~m}^2$ is placed at right angles to a magnetic field of induction $0.05 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$. If the field is decreased to $20 \%$ of its original value in 10 second, the e.m.f. induced in the coil will be
questions.solution:
Faraday’s Law gives the induced e.m.f. as $ε = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$, where magnetic flux is $\Phi_B = B A \cos\theta$. The coil is perpendicular to the field so $\theta = 0^\circ$ and $\cos\theta = 1$. Area $A = 3~\mathrm{m}^2$ remains constant.

The magnetic field decreases from $B_1 = 0.05~\mathrm{Wb}/\mathrm{m}^2$ to $B_2 = 0.01~\mathrm{Wb}/\mathrm{m}^2$ over $\Delta t = 10~\mathrm{s}$, giving $\Delta B = -0.04~\mathrm{Wb}/\mathrm{m}^2$.

The change in flux is $\Delta\Phi_B = A \cdot \Delta B = 3 \times (-0.04) = -0.12~\mathrm{Wb}$.

The induced e.m.f. is $\varepsilon = -\frac{\Delta\Phi_B}{\Delta t} = -\frac{-0.12}{10} = 0.012~\mathrm{V}$.

Converting to millivolts: $0.012~\mathrm{V} = 12~\mathrm{mV}$.

Final answer: $12~\mathrm{mV}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil having ' N ' turns and resistance ' R ' $\Omega$ is connected to a galvanometer of resistance '6R' $\Omega$. The magnetic flux linked with this coil changes from $\phi_1$ weber to $\phi_2$ weber in time ' $t$ ' second. The induced current in the circuit is
questions.solution:
The induced current $I$ is determined by the induced EMF and the total circuit resistance.

With coil resistance $R$ and galvanometer resistance $6R$ in series, the total resistance is $R_{\text{total}} = R + 6R = 7R$.

Faraday's law gives the magnitude of induced EMF as $|\varepsilon| = N \frac{\phi_2 - \phi_1}{t}$ for flux change $\phi_2 - \phi_1$ over time $t$.

Applying Ohm's law yields $I = \frac{|\varepsilon|}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{N(\phi_2 - \phi_1)}{7Rt}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The current flowing through an inductor of self-inductance ' L ' is continuously increasing at constant rate. The variation of induced e.m.f. (e) versus $\mathrm{dI} / \mathrm{dt}$ is shown graphically by graph
questions.solution:
The induced electromotive force in an inductor of self-inductance $L$ is given by $e = -L \frac{dI}{dt}$, where $e$ represents the induced e.m.f. and $\frac{dI}{dt}$ is the rate of change of current.

This relationship shows that $e$ is proportional to $\frac{dI}{dt}$ and that the negative sign indicates opposition to current change according to Lenz's law.

Graph (A) shows $e$ as constant, which contradicts the dependence on $\frac{dI}{dt}$.
Graph (B) shows a straight line through the origin.
Given its positive direction downward, $e_{\text{down}} = k \frac{dI}{dt}$ where $k \gt 0$, so $e_{\text{standard}} = -e_{\text{down}} = -k \frac{dI}{dt}$, matching the formula with $k = L$.
Graph (C) is non-linear, which is incorrect.
Graph (D) implies $e = +L \frac{dI}{dt}$, violating Lenz's law.

Thus, the correct representation is graph (B).

Final answer: $\boxed{B}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical coaxial circular loops carry current 'i' each circulating in the clockwise direction. If the loops are approaching each other, then
options: current in each loop remain the same.
current in one loop increases and in the other it decreases.
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux through each coaxial circular loop increases as they approach each other.

For each loop, the induced current opposes this increasing flux. The original clockwise current produces a magnetic field directed into the plane. To oppose the flux increase, the induced current must generate a field directed out of the plane, requiring an anticlockwise current direction.

Since the induced current opposes the original current, the net current in each loop decreases.

The current in each loop $i$ therefore decreases as they approach.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The plot of magnetic flux ' $\phi$ ' linked with the coil versus current ' $I$ ' is as shown in figure for two inductors $L_1$ and $L_2$. The self inductance of
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux $\phi$ through a coil relates to the current $I$ by $\phi = LI$, where $L$ denotes the self-inductance. On a $\phi$ vs. $I$ graph, this is a linear equation of the form $y = mx$, so the slope corresponds to $L$.

Since the line for $L_1$ is steeper than that for $L_2$, its slope—and thus its self-inductance—is greater. Therefore, $L_1 \gt L_2$.

The correct choice is $\boxed{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long rectangular conducting loop of width ' $\ell$ ', mass ' m ' and resistance ' R ' is placed partly in a perpendicular magnetic field ' B '. It is pushed downwards with velocity ' $V$ ' so that it may continue to fall freely. The velocity ' $V$ ' is
questions.solution:
The velocity $V$ at which the loop falls freely is determined by the terminal velocity condition where the magnetic force balances the gravitational force.

The induced electromotive force due to the motion in the magnetic field $B$ is $e = B \ell V$.

Using Ohm’s law, the induced current becomes $I = \frac{e}{R} = \frac{B \ell V}{R}$.

The resulting upward magnetic force is $F_m = B I \ell = \frac{B^2 \ell^2 V}{R}$.

Setting this equal to the gravitational force $mg$ gives $\frac{B^2 \ell^2 V}{R} = mg$.

Solving for $V$ yields $V = \frac{mgR}{B^2 \ell^2}$.

Among the options, this corresponds to choice C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils P and Q are kept near each other. When no current flows through coil P and current increases in coil Q at the rate $10 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{s}$, the emf in coil P is 12 mV . When coil Q carries no current and current of 1.5 A flows through coil P , the magnetic flux linked with the coil Q in mWb is
questions.solution:
Mutual inductance governs the interaction between the coils. From the induced emf in coil P, $E_P = 12 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{V}$, due to the rate of change of current in coil Q, $\frac{dI_Q}{dt} = 10 \, \text{A/s}$, we apply $E_P = M \frac{dI_Q}{dt}$.

$12 \times 10^{-3} = M \cdot 10$
$M = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{H}$

For a current $I_P = 1.5 \, \text{A}$ in coil P, the magnetic flux linked with coil Q is $\Phi_Q = M I_P$.

$\Phi_Q = (1.2 \times 10^{-3}) \cdot 1.5 = 1.8 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{Wb}$

Converting to milliwebers, $1.8 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{Wb} = 1.8 \, \text{mWb}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{1.8}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When magnetic flux changes from $6.5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~Wb}$ to $11 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~Wb}$ and the change in current is 0.03 A , the coefficient of mutual inductance will be
questions.solution:
The coefficient of mutual inductance relates the change in magnetic flux to the change in current through $\Delta\Phi = M \Delta I$.

The flux increases from $6.5 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Wb}$ to $11 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Wb}$, yielding a change of $\Delta\Phi = (11 - 6.5) \times 10^{-2} = 4.5 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

With $\Delta I = 0.03\ \mathrm{A}$, the mutual inductance is

$M = \frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta I} = \frac{4.5 \times 10^{-2}}{0.03} = 1.5\ \mathrm{H}$

This value corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two circuits $A$ and $B$ are connected to identical d.c. sources each of e.m.f. 10 volt. Self-inductances of circuits $A$ and $B$ are respectively $L_A=10 H$ and $L_B=10 \mathrm{mH}$. The total resistance of each circuit is $40 \Omega$. The ratio of energy consumed in circuit A and circuit B to build up the current to steady value is
questions.solution:
To determine the ratio of energy consumed in circuits A and B while building up the current to a steady value, the energy stored in the inductor at steady state is compared. The energy stored is given by $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$, where $L$ is the self-inductance and $I$ is the steady-state current.

The steady-state current is identical for both circuits due to the same emf of $10 \text{ V}$ and total resistance of $40 \Omega$, resulting in $I_0 = \frac{10}{40} = 0.25$ A.

Circuit A has $L_A = 10$ H, so the energy is $U_A = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 10 \cdot (0.25)^2 = 0.3125$ J.

Circuit B has $L_B = 10$ mH = $0.01$ H, thus $U_B = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0.01 \cdot (0.25)^2 = 0.0003125$ J.

The ratio is $\frac{U_A}{U_B} = \frac{0.3125}{0.0003125} = 1000$.

The ratio is therefore 1000, symbolizing that the energy consumed in circuit A is a thousand times greater than in circuit B.

Answer: $1000$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A magnetic field $4 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~T}$ acts at right angles to a coil of area $100 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ with 50 turns. The average e.m.f. induced in the coil is 0.1 V , when it is removed from the field in time ' $t$ '. The value of ' $t$ ' is
questions.solution:
Faraday's law gives the average induced emf as $\varepsilon = N \left| \frac{\Delta \Phi_B}{\Delta t} \right|$. The magnetic flux through a coil perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field is $\Phi_B = B \cdot A$.

The area is $A = 100 \mathrm{cm}^2 = 10^{-2} \mathrm{m}^2$. The initial flux is $\Phi_i = (4 \times 10^{-2}) \cdot (10^{-2}) = 4 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{Wb}$ and final flux is zero, so $\Delta \Phi_B = -4 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{Wb}$.

Substituting $N = 50$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1 \mathrm{V}$, we get $0.1 = 50 \cdot \frac{4 \times 10^{-4}}{t}$.

Solving for $t$: $t = \frac{50 \cdot 4 \times 10^{-4}}{0.1} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{10^{-1}} = 2 \times 10^{-1} = 0.2 \mathrm{s}$.

The correct answer is $\boxed{0.2}$ second.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper ring having a cut such as not to form a complete loop is held horizontally and a bar magnet is dropped through the ring with its length along the axis of the ring as shown in figure. The acceleration of the falling magnet is ( $g=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Analysis of Magnet Falling Through Cut Ring

When a magnet falls through a conducting ring, Faraday's law indicates that a changing magnetic flux induces an electromotive force. For a current to flow, however, the circuit must form a closed loop.

Since the copper ring has a cut, it cannot sustain an induced current. Without current, no opposing magnetic field is generated via Lenz's law.

The magnet experiences only gravitational acceleration, $g$, as no electromagnetic force opposes its motion.

Thus, the correct choice is $\boxed{A}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of wire of radius ' $r$ ' has 600 turns and a self-inductance of 108 mH . The self-inductance of a coil with same radius and 500 turns is
questions.solution:
The self-inductance $L$ of a coil is proportional to the square of its number of turns: $L \propto N^2$.

Given initial values $L_1 = 108\text{ mH}$ and $N_1 = 600$, and final turns $N_2 = 500$, the inductance becomes:

$L_2 = L_1 \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^2 = 108 \left(\frac{500}{600}\right)^2 = 108 \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 = 108 \cdot \frac{25}{36}$

$L_2 = 3 \cdot 25 = 75\text{ mH}$

Final answer: $75\text{ mH}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of ' $n$ ' turns and resistance $R \Omega$ is connected in series with a resistance $\frac{R}{2}$. The combination is moved for time 't' second through magnetic flux $\Phi_1$ to $\Phi_2$. The induced current in the circuit is
questions.solution:
Induced current in the circuit

The total resistance is the sum of the coil resistance $R$ and the series resistance $\frac{R}{2}$, giving $R_{\text{total}} = \frac{3R}{2}$.

The magnitude of the induced EMF from Faraday's law is $\varepsilon = n \frac{(\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{t}$, where the flux changes from $\Phi_1$ to $\Phi_2$ in time $t$.

Applying Ohm's law, the induced current is $I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{n (\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{t} \times \frac{2}{3R} = \frac{2n (\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{3Rt}$.

This matches option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The equivalent inductance between A and B is equal to
questions.solution:
Equivalent inductance calculation between points A and B

The circuit simplifies when recognizing that all four inductors connect between common nodes N (A and D) and M (C and B). This places the 2H, 3H, 4H, and 6H inductors in parallel.

The equivalent inductance $L_{eq}$ for parallel inductors satisfies:

$\frac{1}{L_{eq}} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{6}$

Combining fractions with common denominator 12:

$\frac{1}{L_{eq}} = \frac{6 + 4 + 3 + 2}{12} = \frac{15}{12} = \frac{5}{4}$

Thus, $L_{eq} = \frac{4}{5}$ H, corresponding to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A square of side ' $L$ ' metre lies in $x-y$ plane in a region where the magnetic field is $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{B}=B_0(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k})$, where $B_0$ is constant. The magnitude of flux passing through the square (in weber) is
questions.solution:
Magnetic flux $\Phi$ through a surface is defined as the dot product of magnetic field $\mathrm{B}$ and area vector $\mathrm{A}$: $\Phi = \mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{A}$.

Given the square in the $x$–$y$ plane with side length $L$, its area vector is $\mathrm{A} = L^2 \hat{k}$.

For magnetic field $\mathrm{B} = B_0(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k})$, the dot product with $\mathrm{A}$ simplifies due to orthogonality of unit vectors:

$\Phi = B_0(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}) \cdot (L^2 \hat{k}) = B_0 L^2 (4\hat{k} \cdot \hat{k}) = 4 B_0 L^2$.

The magnetic flux through the square is $\Phi = 4 B_0 L^2$.

This matches option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of ' n ' turns and area ' A ' is suddenly removed from a magnetic field, a charge ' $q$ ' flows through the coil. If resistance of the coil is ' $R$ ' then the magnetic flux density is (in $\mathrm{Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$ )
questions.solution:
The induced charge flow results from the change in magnetic flux linkage through the coil as it is removed from the field.

The initial magnetic flux linkage is $\Phi_i = nBA$, assuming perpendicular orientation. After removal, $\Phi_f = 0$, giving a total flux change $\Delta\Phi = -nBA$.

By Faraday's law, the induced EMF is $\varepsilon = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$, so the current becomes $I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R} = -\frac{1}{R}\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$.

The total charge transferred during the process is $q = \int I dt = -\frac{1}{R} \int_{\Phi_i}^{\Phi_f} d\Phi = -\frac{1}{R}(\Phi_f - \Phi_i) = \frac{nBA}{R}$.

Solving for $B$ yields $B = \frac{qR}{nA}$.

This corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of $n$ turns and resistance $R \Omega$ is connected in series with resistance $\mathrm{R} / 4$. The combination is moved for time t second through magnetic flux $\phi_1$ to $\phi_2$. The induced current in the circuit is
questions.solution:
The total circuit resistance combines the coil resistance $R$ with the series resistor of $R/4$:

$R_{\text{total}} = R + \frac{R}{4} = \frac{5R}{4}$

By Faraday's law, the magnitude of induced EMF is $E = n \frac{\Delta \phi}{t} = n \frac{(\phi_1 - \phi_2)}{t}$, as the flux decreases from $\phi_1$ to $\phi_2$.

Applying Ohm’s law yields the current:

$I = \frac{E}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{n (\phi_1 - \phi_2)}{t} \cdot \frac{4}{5R} = \frac{4n (\phi_1 - \phi_2)}{5Rt}$

The resulting expression corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical coils of inductance L joined in series are placed very close to each other such that the winding direction of one coil is exactly opposite to that of the other. The net inductance is
questions.solution:
Net inductance for series-connected coils is $L_{\text{net}} = L_1 + L_2 \pm 2M$, where the sign depends on magnetic field alignment.

With identical coils, $L_1 = L_2 = L$. Opposite winding directions produce opposing magnetic fields, indicating subtractive coupling: $L_{\text{net}} = L + L - 2M$.

Identical coils in close proximity with opposing windings achieve perfect coupling ($k=1$), so $M = L$.

$L_{\text{net}} = 2L - 2L = 0$

The net inductance is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a current in the conducting coil is changed from 5 A in one direction to 5 A in opposite direction in 0.5 second, an average induced e.m.f in the coil is 2 V . The self-inductance of the coil is
questions.solution:
The induced eMF in a coil due to self-inductance follows $E = -L \frac{dI}{dt}$, where $L$ represents the self-inductance and $\frac{dI}{dt}$ the rate of current change. Given the initial current $I_1 = 5$ A and final current $I_2 = -5$ A, the current change is $\Delta I = -10$ A over $\Delta t = 0.5$ s, with an average induced eMF magnitude of $2$ V.

The magnitude equation simplifies to $E_{\text{avg}} = L \left| \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \right|$. Substituting values gives $2 = L \left| \frac{-10}{0.5} \right| = L \times 20$, leading to $L = \frac{2}{20} = 0.1$ H.

Converting to millihenrys yields $L = 0.1 \times 1000 = 100$ mH.

The self-inductance is 100 mH, corresponding to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Figure shows the north pole of a magnet moving away from a thick conducting loop containing a capacitor. The excess positive charge will arrive on
questions.solution:
Magnetic flux analysis: The north pole moving away decreases rightward magnetic flux through the loop.

Lenz's Law application: The induced current must generate a magnetic field opposing this decrease, pointing rightward through the loop.

Current direction: A rightward magnetic field requires a clockwise current when viewed from the right.

Capacitor charge accumulation: Clockwise current flows toward terminal $b$ through the right side and from terminal $a$ through the left side, implying current flows from $a$ to $b$ through the capacitor. Positive charge accumulates on plate $a$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A graph of magnetic flux $(\phi)$ versus current $(\mathrm{I})$ is shown for four inductors P, Q R, S. The largest value of self-inductance is for inductor
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux $\phi$ through an inductor is directly proportional to the current $I$, with self-inductance $L$ as the constant: $\phi = LI$.

Hence, $L = \frac{\phi}{I}$, which corresponds to the slope of the $\phi$ versus $I$ graph. A steeper slope indicates greater self-inductance.

From the graph, line P has the steepest slope, followed by Q, then R, and finally S with the least steep slope.

Inductor P has the largest self-inductance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The total charge induced in a conducting loop when it is moved in a uniform magnetic field depends on
options: the total change in magnetic flux.
the rate of change of magnetic flux.
questions.solution:
The induced charge in a conducting loop is determined by Faraday's law and Ohm's law. The induced electromotive force $E = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ drives a current $I = \frac{E}{R} = -\frac{1}{R}\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$ through the loop.

Integrating this current over time gives the total charge: $q = \int I dt = -\frac{1}{R} \int d\Phi = -\frac{1}{R}(\Phi_f - \Phi_i)$.

Hence $|q| = \frac{|\Delta\Phi|}{R}$, showing that the total induced charge depends only on the net change in magnetic flux and the loop's resistance.

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper ring is held horizontally and a bar magnet is dropped through the ring with its length along the axis of the ring. The acceleration of the falling magnet while it is passing through the ring is
options: more than acceleration due to gravity.
less than acceleration due to gravity.
depends on the diameter of ring and length of magnet.
depends on pole strength of magnet.
questions.solution:
The falling magnet induces a current in the copper ring due to changing magnetic flux. According to Lenz's Law, the induced current always opposes the motion causing it, creating an upward electromagnetic force that counteracts gravity.

This results in a net downward force $F_{\text{net}} = mg - F_{\text{em}}$, where $F_{\text{em}} \gt 0$. Since acceleration $a = F_{\text{net}}/m$, we have $a \lt g$.

The magnet therefore falls with acceleration less than $g$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of resistance $400 \Omega$ is placed in a magnetic field. If the magnetic flux ' $\phi$ ' (Wb) linked with the coil varies with time ' $t$ ' (s) as $\phi=50 t^2+4$, the current in the coil at $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$ will be
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux linkage is given by $\phi = 50t^2 + 4$ Wb. Faraday's law gives the induced EMF as $\varepsilon = -\frac{d\phi}{dt} = -\frac{d}{dt}(50t^2 + 4)$.

The derivative is $\frac{d\phi}{dt} = 100t$, so the EMF becomes $\varepsilon = -100t$ V. At time $t = 2$ s, we have $\varepsilon = -100 \times 2 = -200$ V, giving a magnitude of $|\varepsilon| = 200$ V.

Using Ohm's law $I = \frac{|\varepsilon|}{R}$ with $R = 400 \Omega$, the current is $I = \frac{200}{400} = 0.5$ A.

Final answer: $0.5$ A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil is wound on a core of rectangular cross-section. If all the linear dimensions of core are increased by a factor 3 and number of turns per unit length of coil remains same, the self-inductance increases by a factor
questions.solution:
The self-inductance of a solenoid is given by $L = \mu n^2 A l$, where $\mu$ denotes permeability of the core material, $n$ the number of turns per unit length, $A$ the cross-sectional area, and $l$ the length of the solenoid.

All linear dimensions of the core's cross-section increase by a factor of 3. Since $A$ scales with the square of linear dimensions, the new area becomes $A' = (3)^2 A = 9A$. The length $l$ remains constant, as this scaling applies only to cross-sectional dimensions.

Substituting into the inductance formula yields $L' = \mu n^2 (9A) l = 9(\mu n^2 A l) = 9L$.

The self-inductance therefore increases by a factor of 9.

$\boxed{D}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A conducting ring of certain resistance is falling towards a current carrying straight long conductor. The ring and conductor are in the same plane. Then
options: induced current in the coil is zero.
induced current in the coil is anticlockwise.
induced current in the coil is clockwise.
questions.solution:
The induced current direction is determined by applying Faraday's Law and Lenz's Law.

The magnetic field above a rightward-carrying conductor points out of the page, as given by the right-hand thumb rule. As the ring falls toward the conductor, the magnetic field strength $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ increases since distance $r$ decreases. This results in an increasing magnetic flux directed out of the page through the ring.

Lenz's Law requires that the induced current opposes this flux increase. The induced current must therefore produce a magnetic field directed into the page. Applying the right-hand curl rule shows that this corresponds to a clockwise current in the ring.

The induced current flows clockwise.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the phase difference between the flux linked with a coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field and the induced e.m.f. produced in it?
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux linked with a coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field is $\Phi = BA \cos(\omega t)$.

Faraday's law gives $\epsilon = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Differentiating $\Phi$, we obtain $\epsilon = BA\omega \sin(\omega t)$.

Using the identity $\sin(\omega t) = \cos(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2})$, the e.m.f. becomes $\epsilon = BA\omega \cos(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2})$.

The flux has phase $\omega t$ while the e.m.f. has phase $\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}$, so the e.m.f. lags the flux by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ radians.

The phase difference is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two coils P and Q are kept near each other. When no current flows through coil $P$ and current increases in coil $Q$ at the rate of $10 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{s}$, the e.m.f. in coil $P$ is 15 mV. When coil $Q$ carries no current and current of 1.8 A flows through coil P, the magnetic flux linked with coil Q is
questions.solution:
The mutual inductance $M$ is determined from the induced emf in coil P due to the changing current in coil Q. Given $E_P = 15 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{V}$ and $\frac{dI_Q}{dt} = 10 \, \text{A}/\text{s}$, the relationship $E_P = M \frac{dI_Q}{dt}$ yields $M = \frac{15 \times 10^{-3}}{10} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{H}$.

The magnetic flux $\Phi_Q$ linked with coil Q when a current $I_P = 1.8 \, \text{A}$ flows through coil P is $\Phi_Q = M I_P = (1.5 \times 10^{-3}) \cdot 1.8 = 2.7 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{Wb}$, or $2.7 \, \text{mWb}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{2.7 \, \text{mWb}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: To manufacture a solenoid of length ' $\ell$ ' and inductance ' $L$ ', the length of the thin wire required is (Diameter of the solenoid is very less than length, $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
The self-inductance of a long solenoid is given by $L = \mu_0 n^2 A \ell$, where $n$ is turns per unit length and $A$ is cross-sectional area.

Expressing $n = N/\ell$ and $A = \pi r^2$ yields $L = \mu_0 (N/\ell)^2 (\pi r^2) \ell = \mu_0 N^2 \pi r^2 / \ell$.

The wire length for $N$ turns of radius $r$ is $L_{wire} = 2\pi r N$, so $N = L_{wire}/(2\pi r)$.

Substituting gives $L = \frac{\mu_0}{\ell} \left(\frac{L_{wire}}{2\pi r}\right)^2 \pi r^2 = \frac{\mu_0 L_{wire}^2}{4\pi \ell}$.

Solving for $L_{wire}$ results in $L_{wire} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi \ell L}{\mu_0}}$, matching option A.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Initially a rectangular coil with length vertical is moving out with constant velocity 'v' in a constant magnetic field 'B' towards right. Now the same coil is rotated through $90^{\circ}$ in same plane in same magnetic field $B$ and the coil is moving with same velocity $v$. The magnitude of induced e.m.f. is now
options: sometimes greater and sometimes less than initial induced e.m.f.
questions.solution:
For a conductor moving perpendicular to a magnetic field, the induced e.m.f. is governed by $\varepsilon = B l v$, where $l$ is the length cutting flux lines perpendicularly.

The rectangular coil has dimensions $L$ (length) and $w$ (width). Initially, with $L$ vertical, the induced e.m.f. is $\varepsilon_{\text{initial}} = B L v$.

After a $90^\circ$ rotation, the vertical side becomes $w$, so $\varepsilon_{\text{final}} = B w v$.

The magnitudes compare as $\varepsilon_{\text{final}} \gt \varepsilon_{\text{initial}}$ if $w \gt L$, $\varepsilon_{\text{final}} \lt \varepsilon_{\text{initial}}$ if $w \lt L$, and are equal if $w = L$. Since no dimensions are specified, all outcomes are possible, leading to answer $\boxed{D}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A simple pendulum with bob of mass $m$ and conducting wire of length L swings under gravity through an angle $\theta$. The component of earth's magnetic field in the direction perpendicular to swing is B. Maximum e.m.f. induced across the pendulum is ( $g=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
The maximum induced electromotive force occurs when the pendulum bob attains its maximum velocity at the lowest point of its swing, where the motion is perpendicular to the magnetic field. The induced emf is given by $ε = BLv$, with $v$ representing the instantaneous velocity perpendicular to the field.

Using conservation of energy, the gravitational potential energy at maximum displacement converts entirely to kinetic energy at the lowest point. The vertical drop from maximum angular displacement $θ$ is $h = L(1 - \cosθ) = 2L\sin^2(θ/2)$.

From $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv_{\text{max}}^2$, the maximum velocity is $v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{2gh} = 2\sin(θ/2)\sqrt{gL}$.

Substituting into the emf expression yields the maximum induced emf:

$ε_{\text{max}} = BL \cdot 2\sin(θ/2)\sqrt{gL} = 2BL\sqrt{gL}\sin(θ/2)$

This result corresponds to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three inductances are connected as shown in the figure. The equivalent inductance between $A$ and $B$ is
questions.solution:
Equivalent inductance between points A and B

The circuit contains two 0.7 H inductors in parallel, which are then in series with a 0.85 H inductor.

For parallel inductors, the equivalent is $L_p = \frac{L_1 \cdot L_2}{L_1 + L_2} = \frac{0.7 \cdot 0.7}{0.7 + 0.7} = \frac{0.49}{1.4} = 0.35$ H.

The total inductance is then $L_{eq} = L_p + L_3 = 0.35 + 0.85 = 1.20$ H.

This matches option B of $1.20$ H.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A coil of self-inductance $L$ is connected in series with a bulb and an a.c. source. Brightness of the bulb decreases when
options: an iron rod is inserted in the coil.
frequency of a.c. source is decreased.
number of turns in the coil is reduced.
a capacitance of reactance $\left(X_C-X_L\right)$ is included in the same circuit.
questions.solution:
The brightness of the bulb depends on the power dissipated, given by $P = I^2 R$, so it decreases when the RMS current $I$ decreases.

In an AC series circuit with the bulb (resistance $R$) and coil (inductive reactance $X_L$), the impedance is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$ and the current is $I = V/Z$. A decrease in current requires an increase in impedance, which occurs when $X_L$ increases since $X_L = 2\pi f L$.

Inserting an iron rod into the coil increases the magnetic permeability, raising the inductance $L$. This increases $X_L$, thus increasing $Z$ and decreasing $I$, which reduces brightness.

Decreasing the AC source frequency reduces $X_L$, decreasing $Z$ and increasing both $I$ and brightness.

Reducing the number of turns in the coil decreases $L$ (since $L \propto N^2$), reducing $X_L$ and $Z$, and increasing brightness.

Including a capacitance with specified reactance leads to impedance $Z' = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, which may increase or decrease depending on $X_C$. Since brightness reduction is not guaranteed, this option is incorrect.

The correct choice is $\boxed{A}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The current flowing through an inductor of self-inductance L is continuously increasing at constant rate. The variation of induced e.m.f. (e) verses $\mathrm{dI} / \mathrm{dt}$ is shown graphically by figure
questions.solution:
The induced electromotive force (e.m.f.) in an inductor is given by Faraday's law:

$e = -L \frac{dI}{dt}$

where $L$ is the self-inductance (a positive constant) and $\frac{dI}{dt}$ is the rate of change of current.

The equation indicates a linear relationship where the e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of current change.
The negative sign reflects Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. opposes changes in current.
When $\frac{dI}{dt} \gt 0$, the e.m.f. is negative; when $\frac{dI}{dt} \lt 0$, the e.m.f. is positive.

The graph of $e$ versus $\frac{dI}{dt}$ must be a straight line through the origin with negative slope $-L$.

Analysis of the options:
Option A shows constant negative e.m.f. for positive $\frac{dI}{dt}$, inconsistent with proportionality.
Option B displays the correct linear relationship through the origin with negative slope.
Option C shows a nonlinear relationship, which is incorrect.
Option D has positive slope, contradicting Lenz's law.

Thus, graph B correctly represents $e = -L \frac{dI}{dt}$.

The correct choice is $\boxed{B}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The coefficient of mutual induction is 2 H and induced e.m.f. across secondary is 2 kV . Current in the primary is reduced from 6 A to 3 A . The time required for the change of current is
questions.solution:
Using the formula for induced electromotive force, $\varepsilon = M \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$, with mutual inductance $M = 2\text{ H}$, e.m.f. $\varepsilon = 2000\text{ V}$, and current change $\Delta I = 3\text{ A}$, we solve for the time interval:

$\Delta t = \frac{M \Delta I}{\varepsilon} = \frac{2 \times 3}{2000}$

Simplifying gives $\Delta t = 0.003\text{ s}$ or $3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$, which corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two planar concentric rings of metal wire having radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ ( $r_1\gt r_2$ ) are placed in air. The current I is flowing through the coil of larger radius. The mutual inductance between the coils is given by ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
The mutual inductance between two concentric coaxial circular coils is determined by the magnetic flux linkage. The magnetic field at the center of the larger coil of radius $r_1$ carrying current $I$ is $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r_1}$.

Since the coils are coaxial and planar with $r_1 \gt r_2$, this field is uniform over the smaller coil's area $\pi r_2^2$. The resulting flux is $\Phi_2 = B_1 \cdot \pi r_2^2 = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2 I}{2r_1}$.

Mutual inductance is defined as $M = \frac{\Phi_2}{I} = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2r_1}$, corresponding to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Out of the following which law obeys the law of conservation of energy?
questions.solution:
Lenz's law provides a direct application of energy conservation in electromagnetic induction. When magnetic flux through a circuit changes, the induced EMF generates a current whose magnetic field opposes the original flux change. This opposition prevents energy from being created or destroyed without external work.

$\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$

If the induced current reinforced rather than opposed the flux change, it would create a self-amplifying effect violating energy conservation. The negative sign in Faraday's law formulation embodies this energy conservation principle.

Kirchhoff's junction rule conserves charge, Ampere's law describes magnetostatics, and Gauss's law relates electric flux to charge—none directly express energy conservation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic flux through a coil is $4 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~Wb}$ at time $\mathrm{t}=0$. It reduces to $30 \%$ of its original value in time $t$ second. If e.m.f. induced in the coil is 0.56 mV then the value of $t$ is
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux through the coil at t = 0 is $\Phi_1 = 4 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Wb}$, which reduces to $30\%$ of its initial value, giving $\Phi_2 = 0.30 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

The change in flux is $\Delta\Phi = \Phi_2 - \Phi_1 = -2.8 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

Using Faraday's law, $\varepsilon = -\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, and the given $\varepsilon = 0.56 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V}$, we substitute:

$0.56 \times 10^{-3} = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{t}$

Solving for t, $t = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{0.56 \times 10^{-3}} = 5 \times 10^{-1} = 0.5\ \mathrm{s}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $L$ is the inductance and $R$ is the resistance then the SI unit of $\frac{L}{R}$ is
questions.solution:
SI Unit of $\frac{L}{R}$

The SI unit of resistance $R$ is derived from Ohm's law, $R = \frac{V}{I}$, giving Volts per Ampere.

Inductance $L$ is defined by $V = L \frac{dI}{dt}$, so $L = \frac{V}{dI/dt}$. Since the unit of $\frac{dI}{dt}$ is Amperes per second, the unit of $L$ is Volt-seconds per Ampere.

Thus, $\frac{L}{R} = \frac{(\text{V} \cdot \text{s} / \text{A})}{(\text{V} / \text{A})} = \text{s}$.

This time constant $\tau = \frac{L}{R}$ has SI unit second, confirming the dimensional consistency.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$ (Note: The answer should be "second", but the provided box states A, which may be a typographical error; the correct unit is seconds.)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When three inductors of same inductance 'L' are connected in series and 'I' is the current passing through the circuit. The energy stored in the circuit is
questions.solution:
For three inductors of inductance $L$ connected in series, the equivalent inductance becomes $L_{eq} = L + L + L = 3L$.

The energy stored in an inductor is given by $U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$. Substituting the equivalent inductance yields $U = \frac{1}{2} (3L) I^2 = \frac{3}{2} L I^2$.

This result corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The self-inductance of a circuit is numerically equal to
options: the work done in establishing the magnetic flux associated with circuit.
twice the work done in establishing the magnetic flux associated with unit current in the circuit.
thrice the work done in establishing the magnetic flux associated with unit current in the circuit.
the work done in establishing the magnetic flux associated with unit current in the circuit.
questions.solution:
The self-inductance $L$ represents twice the work required to establish the magnetic flux associated with unit current in the circuit.

The energy stored in an inductor with current $I$ is $U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$. For unit current ($I = 1$), this becomes $U_{\text{unit}} = \frac{1}{2}L$, yielding $L = 2U_{\text{unit}}$.

This corresponds directly with option B.

$\boxed{B}$

questions.q: If number of turns per unit length in a solenoid is tripled, the self inductance of solenoid will
questions.solution:
Self-inductance of a solenoid is given by
$\begin{aligned}
& \quad \mathrm{L}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{~N}^2 \mathrm{~A}}{l} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{~L} \propto \mathrm{~N}^2 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{~L}_1}{\mathrm{~L}_2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{N}_1}{\mathrm{~N}_2}\right)^2 \\

questions.q: A closely wound coil of 100 turns and of crosssection $1 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ has coefficient of self inductance 1 mH . The magnetic induction at the centre of the core of a coil when a current of 2 A flows in it, will be (in $\mathrm{Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$ )
questions.solution:
Given that, $\mathrm{N}=100, \quad \mathrm{~A}=1 \mathrm{~cm}^2=1 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$, $\mathrm{L}=1 \mathrm{mH}=1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{H}$ and $\mathrm{I}=2 \mathrm{~A}$ Now, self-inductance of a coil is given by, $\mathrm{L}=\mu_0 \frac{\mathrm{~N}^2 \mathrm{~A}}{1}...(i)$
Where $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space $=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{H} / \mathrm{m}$ and $l$ is the length of the coil Also, magnetic induction B in the core, $\mathrm{B}=\mu_0 \frac{\mathrm{NI}}{l}$ From equation (i), $\begin{aligned} & l=\mu_0 \frac{\mathrm{~N}^2 \mathrm{~A}}{\mathrm{~L}}=\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right) \frac{(100)^2 \times 1 \times 10^{-4}}{1 \times 10^{-3}} \\ & \quad=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10^4 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^3 \\ & l=4 \pi \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$
Substituting this in equation (ii), $\begin{aligned} B & =\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right) \frac{100 \times 2}{4 \pi \times 10^{-3}} \\ & =10^{-7} \times 200 \times 10^3=0.2 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2 \end{aligned}$

questions.q: The coefficient of mutual induction is 2 H and induced e.m.f. across secondary is 2 kV . Current in the primary is reduced from 6 A to 3 A . The time required for the change of current is
questions.solution:
Using the formula for induced electromotive force, $\varepsilon = M \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$, with mutual inductance $M = 2\text{ H}$, e.m.f. $\varepsilon = 2000\text{ V}$, and current change $\Delta I = 3\text{ A}$, we solve for the time interval:

$\Delta t = \frac{M \Delta I}{\varepsilon} = \frac{2 \times 3}{2000}$

Simplifying gives $\Delta t = 0.003\text{ s}$ or $3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$, which corresponds to option D.

questions.solution: $\begin{array}{ll} & \text { Given } \mathrm{I}=4 \mathrm{~A}, \mathrm{~N}=400 \text { and } \\ & \phi=3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~Wb} \\ & \mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{LdI}}{\mathrm{dt}} \cdot \text { and } \mathrm{e}=\frac{\mathrm{Nd} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \frac{\mathrm{Nd} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{LdI}}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{N} \phi=\mathrm{LI} \\ & \mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{N} \phi}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{400 \times 3 \times 10^{-3}}{4}=0.3 \mathrm{H} \\ \therefore \quad & \text { Energy stored in the coil }=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{LI}^2 \\ = & \frac{1}{2} \times 0.3 \times 16 \\ = & 2.4 \mathrm{~J}\end{array}$

questions.q: Two concentric circular coils having radii ' $r_1$ ' and ' $r_2$ ' $\left(r_2 \ll r_1\right)$ are placed co-axially with centres coinciding. The mutual inductance of the arrangement is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space) (Both coils have single turn)
questions.solution:
The magnetic field at the centre of a loop is given by $B=\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2 R}\therefore \quad$ Magnetic field produced by ring $A, B_A=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_1}\therefore \quad$ Magnetic flux produced in ring B due to $\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{A}}$, $\phi_B=B_A A_B\begin{aligned} & A_B=\pi r_2^2 \\ \therefore \quad & \phi_B \\ = & \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_1} \times \pi r_2^2=\frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2 r_1} I \end{aligned}$
Mutual Inductance $\mathrm{M}=\frac{\phi}{\mathrm{I}}$ (from MI $\phi=\mathrm{M}$ ) $\therefore \quad$ We can write, $M=\frac{\phi_B}{I}=\frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2 \cdot I}{2 r_1 \cdot I}=\frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^2}{2 r_1}$

Using Lenz law,
Induced e.m.f. is given by, $e=-N \frac{d \phi}{d t}$
Change in magnetic flux $=\frac{\mathrm{d} \phi}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{dB}}{\mathrm{dt}} \mathrm{A} \cos \theta$

& \therefore \quad B=\frac{3}{4} B
\end{aligned}$
Substituting the values,
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{e} & =\frac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta \mathrm{t}} \\

\therefore \quad \mathrm{e} & =\frac{3}{4} \mathrm{AB}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The magnetic flux through a coil of resistance $R$ changes by an amount $\Delta \phi$ in time $\Delta t$. The total quantity of induced electric charge $Q$ is
questions.solution:
From Faraday's law of EMI, emf induced in the circuit is given by,
$e=-\frac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t}$
And if $R$ is the resistance in the circuit then it becomes,
$\begin{aligned} & I=\frac{e}{R} \\ & \quad \Rightarrow I=-\frac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t \cdot R}\end{aligned}$
So, the total amount of charge passing through the circuit will become,
$\begin{aligned} & \because \Delta Q=I \times \Delta t \\ & \Rightarrow \Delta Q=-\frac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t \cdot R} \cdot \Delta t \\ & \Rightarrow \Delta Q=-\frac{\Delta \phi}{R}\end{aligned}$
So, the total amount of charge passing through the circuit is given by $\frac{\Delta \phi}{R}$

For a solinoid magnetic field at the center is:

Total magnetic self flux is:
$\phi=B A N=\mu_0\left(\frac{N}{l}\right) I A N$
According to the definition of magnetic flux and coefficient of self induction:
$\phi=L I$
On comparing the above two expressions, the self-induction of a long solenoid is given by

where, $N=$ number of truns, $L=$ Length and $A=$ cross - sectional area.
Therefore, the self-induction of a long solenoid does not depend upon the current flowing through it.

questions.solution:

The magnetic magnetic field $B$ at the center of a coil carrying current $\mathrm{i}$, with radius $\mathrm{r}$ is given by,
$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 r}$
So for a coil with $\mathrm{n}$ no. of turns: $\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{N}}=\mathrm{N}\left(\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \mathrm{r}}\right)$
The self flux associated with one coil is : $\phi 1=\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{A}$
Now, the self flux associated with coil of $\mathrm{N}$ turns is: $\phi \mathrm{N}=\mathrm{N} \phi_1$
Therefore,
$\phi N=N\left\{N\left(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 r}\right) A\right\}_1$
Now using the definition of self-inductance: $L=\frac{\theta}{I}$, we get, $\mathrm{L} \propto \mathrm{N}^2$
So, self-inductance is proportional to square of number of turns in the coil.

Interference is a phenomenon in which two waves of same frequency superpose to give resultant intensity different from sum of their separate intensity. So, it cannot exhibit particle's nature of light.
(b) Diffraction is a phenomenon in which light bends at sharp ends of an obstacle or a hole. So, it also cannot exhibit particle's nature of light.
(c) Polarisation of light is a property owing to which a light ray after emerging through a crystal (a special kind like tourmaline) have vibrations in a plane perpendicular to its direction of propagation. So, it also can not explain particle's nature of light.
(d) Photoelectric effect states that light travels in the form of bundles or packets of energy, called photons. This effect is explained on the basis of quantum nature of light. So, it clearly explains the particle's nature of light.
Hence, (d) is correct.

While bending of light rays at curvatures of obstacles is called diffraction. Dispersion is splitting of white light and polarisation is the restriction of the vibrations in a transverse wave.
